title: 22 Indian Nationals Aboard Two Vessels Hijacked by Pirates Off Yemen and Somalia
excerpt: Separate piracy attacks seize an oil tanker and a cargo ship carrying Indian crew members as Somali piracy surges amid redirected naval patrols.
body:
• Two commercial vessels carrying a total of 22 Indian nationals have been hijacked in separate piracy incidents off Yemen and Somalia.
  • The Eritrea-flagged tanker M.T. Sibu 1, with 16 Indians among its 20 crew, was seized by six armed pirates in the Gulf of Aden about 30 nautical miles off Yemen.
  • A second vessel, the Cameroon-flagged M/V LUTUF, was captured off Somalia's Puntland coast with six Indian crew members aboard.
  • The hijackings underscore a renewed piracy surge in the Horn of Africa as international naval patrols have been redirected to counter Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.

Two Vessels Seized in Separate Attacks

Two commercial vessels with a combined 22 Indian nationals on board have been hijacked in separate incidents off the coasts of Yemen and Somalia, Indian maritime authorities confirmed on Thursday, underscoring a dangerous resurgence of piracy in waters once patrolled by a robust international naval armada.

The Eritrea-flagged oil products tanker M.T. Sibu 1, carrying 20 crew members including 16 Indian nationals, was seized by six armed pirates in the Gulf of Aden approximately 30 nautical miles off Yemen's coast. The crew also includes one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi national, with the nationality of one additional seafarer yet to be confirmed. All 20 crew members were reported safe at the time of seizure, according to India's Directorate of Maritime Administration, though the latest status of the vessel and crew remains unclear.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations confirmed the tanker had been boarded by armed individuals and diverted toward Somalia from a position 136 nautical miles east of Yemen's Mukalla.

Second Vessel Taken Off Puntland

In a separate incident earlier in the week, pirates captured the Cameroon-flagged cargo vessel M/V LUTUF off Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland coast. The ship, carrying 10 crew members including six Indian nationals, was seized approximately 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland's Eyl district. The crew also included one Turkish national, one Georgian, and two Serbian security guards.

The vessel, owned by Polar Movement Shipping, was reportedly carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu along with communications and satellite equipment, according to a Somali official. It was subsequently taken toward the Nugaal coast.

"I told one person here where I was — the Directorate of Maritime Administration — and provided their details."

— Sumit Kant Singh, SKS Krishiv Marine Services, which recruited four of the M.T. Sibu 1 crew members

Piracy Resurges as Naval Patrols Shift

The twin hijackings mark the latest in a wave of pirate attacks that have swept the Horn of Africa region in recent months. Somali piracy caused havoc along the country's coastline between 2008 and 2018 before a multinational naval campaign largely suppressed the threat. But pirate activity has picked up sharply since late 2023, with multiple vessels seized in the Gulf of Aden and off the Somali coast in 2026 alone.

Security analysts attribute the resurgence to a security vacuum left as international naval assets were redirected to counter Houthi rebel attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The UKMTO has raised the piracy threat level along the Somali coast in response.

In July, the Tanzanian-flagged fuel and chemical tanker MT Asana, carrying 11 Indians among its 19 crew, was hijacked in Yemeni waters and subsequently held by Somali pirates in the Puntland region. The Indian Navy has conducted multiple rescue operations this year, including freeing a hijacked Iranian fishing vessel and assisting crews trapped in citadels aboard besieged ships.

Impact on Indian Seafarers

India is one of the world's largest suppliers of commercial seafarers, with hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals serving on merchant vessels across global shipping lanes. The Gulf of Aden, which connects the Arabian Sea to the Red Sea through the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb, is among the world's busiest and most strategically important waterways.

India's Directorate of Maritime Administration has directed the relevant recruitment agencies to submit incident reports and periodic updates through the e-Navik marine casualty reporting system. The Indian Navy, which maintains a permanent presence in the region through its anti-piracy deployments, has been monitoring the situation.

With at least four vessels hijacked in the region in recent weeks and dozens of Indian seafarers caught in the crossfire, pressure is mounting on New Delhi to push for stronger international coordination to protect commercial shipping lanes in the Horn of Africa.

nri_angle: 22 Indian seafarers are caught in a piracy resurgence that threatens one of the world's largest sources of commercial maritime labor.
